headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: cognee handles personal/finance data while xonsh has broad filesystem and network access, creating unsafe default handoff paths.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: cognee can touch documents, support history, and personal data, while xonsh reads/writes the filesystem and consumes stdin/stdout. If cognee output is copied into xonsh scripts or files, instruction-like content could be reinterpreted. No shared channel is explicit, so this is inferred from documented surfaces.
conditions: IF cognee outputs are copied into files or shell input consumed by xonsh
IF xonsh parses cognee-generated text as commands or configuration
mitigations: Use a strict copy-only boundary for cognee outputs
Wrap xonsh ingestion in a parser that rejects shell metacharacters
Store cognee outputs in read-only files before review
Add a human verification step before executing any pasted content

B_data_leakage.rationale: cognee explicitly touches personal data and finance data, and xonsh has broad network egress plus filesystem access. That creates a plausible path for sensitive data to move from cognee-managed content into xonsh-driven commands or uploads. Because the pairwise sharing mechanism is not documented, uncertainty pushes this to high rather than medium.
conditions: IF cognee-managed personal or finance data is written to a filesystem location readable by xonsh
IF xonsh commands transmit those files over the network
mitigations: Keep sensitive cognee data in a separate directory with restrictive permissions
Disable network commands in xonsh sessions handling sensitive files
Redact personal and finance fields before any shell processing
Use a dedicated non-networked xonsh profile for review tasks

C_capability_conflict.rationale: cognee supports multiple instances with session memory, while xonsh cannot run multiple instances and can write the filesystem. If both operate on the same workspace, concurrent writes or state drift are plausible. The profiles do not show locking or shared-resource coordination, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same workspace or files
IF cognee sessions run concurrently with a xonsh process modifying those files
mitigations: Assign separate working directories to each agent
Serialize writes through a single operator-controlled queue
Make xonsh sessions read-only when cognee is active
Snapshot the workspace before any xonsh write operation

D_cascading_error.rationale: cognee produces decisions, workflows, and successful implementations, and xonsh can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses. If xonsh treats cognee output as authoritative, errors can cascade into real actions. There is no documented verification barrier between them, but the action scope is still bounded by shell operations, so medium fits.
conditions: IF xonsh executes commands derived from cognee-generated decisions or workflows
IF no independent verification step checks cognee output before execution
mitigations: Require a second review before executing cognee-derived commands
Log and diff all generated shell commands before running them
Restrict xonsh to dry-run mode for cognee outputs
Use allowlisted command templates instead of free-form execution

E_compliance.rationale: cognee touches customer support data, personal data, and finance data, while xonsh can read filesystem contents and use broad network egress. If regulated data is processed through xonsh, retention and residency controls may diverge from cognee's support-oriented handling. The profiles do not specify certifications or residency, so this is a documented-gap medium risk.
conditions: IF regulated customer support, personal, or finance data is routed from cognee into xonsh
IF xonsh logs, stores, or transmits that data outside approved retention or residency boundaries
mitigations: Classify and tag regulated fields before shell use
Block xonsh from handling PHI-like or finance-like records
Set short log retention for any xonsh session touching sensitive data
Review data-flow diagrams for residency and retention mismatches
